title: Typing-indicator KV prefetch for hibernated chat sessions
idea: When a response finishes, the server spills that session's KV cache to NVMe/CXL flash. It prefetches the cache back into HBM when the client sends a 'user started typing' or 'tab focused' event. This jumps from the nanosecond scale of HBM to the 5-60 s of human think time between turns, which hides a 10-200 ms restore completely.
why: HBM capacity and data movement (fact 5): live chat sessions are idle more than 90% of wall-clock time, yet their KV dominates inference HBM. Keeping only the actively decoding sessions resident cuts resident KV bytes about 5-15x.

title: Temporal mipmap KV cache with on-demand full-resolution recall
idea: Attention K/V is stored as a pyramid over token time. The last ~2k tokens stay at full resolution. Older spans are pooled into 8- and 64-token summary vectors that stay in HBM, while their full-resolution copies are parked in flash. When a query puts more than a threshold of attention mass on a summary, the controller fetches that span at full resolution for the next step, like texture mipmapping applied to time.
why: Resident KV grows roughly logarithmically instead of linearly with context, needing 5-10x less HBM at 128k-1M tokens while the detail that is needed can still be recalled.

title: Memory whose precision fades with page age
idea: Software tags pages as tolerant (caches, embeddings, KV, media buffers). A memory-controller engine re-quantizes each tolerant page as it ages through epochs of seconds, then minutes, then hours: 16, 8, 4 and finally 2 bits per value, with per-block scales. It releases the frames this frees. Re-access re-promotes the page but cannot restore lost bits, much like the fading of human memory.
why: Tolerant data is 30-60% of the footprint on inference and caching servers. Aging it in time gives 2-4x capacity on those classes.

title: Follow-the-night DRAM provisioning across continents
idea: The global fleet is treated as one memory pool over 24 hours. Deferrable memory-heavy jobs (embedding rebuilds, batch inference, index builds, ETL) are routed to whichever region is in its diurnal trough. Each region's DRAM is then sized for the flattened global curve, not for its local evening peak.
why: Fleets provision DRAM for peak, and diurnal peak-to-trough is 1.5-2x. This means 15-30% fewer DIMMs fleetwide with zero new silicon.

title: Rack-wide lockstep layer broadcast replaces per-server weight copies
idea: One memory sled per rack holds the model weights once. It broadcasts each layer over a multicast optical fabric while all 64 servers execute that same layer in lockstep. Each GPU keeps only a two-layer double buffer of weights. Spatial replication becomes a synchronized schedule in time.
why: Weights are replicated N times today; this makes it one copy per rack. That frees 40-80% of each GPU's HBM for KV, or allows proportionally less HBM per accelerator.

title: Content-addressed CXL switch acting as a rack memory CDN
idea: NICs hash cold 4 KB pages with BLAKE3 and publish them to a CXL switch that keeps a hash-to-physical map in on-switch SRAM. Identical pages from every server in the rack (container layers, libraries, zero pages, model shards, JIT code) collapse into one read-only copy in pooled memory, which every host maps.
why: Dedup on a single host gets 5-15%. Across hosts at rack scale on a homogeneous fleet it can reach 20-40% of the resident footprint.

title: Byte-second pricing for compilers, runtimes and schedulers
idea: Allocators, ML compilers and cluster schedulers optimize byte-seconds (capacity x residency time) instead of peak bytes. The compiler rematerializes or streams any tensor whose recompute energy is lower than the cost of holding it in DRAM for that many byte-seconds, and clusters bill tenants per GB-microsecond actually resident.
why: Moving the metric from space to space x time makes short-lived data cheap and idle long-held data expensive. That gives 2-5x less activation footprint in training and 20-30% at cluster level.

title: Bit-plane progressive memory with mantissa tails in flash
idea: Numeric arrays are stored transposed into bit-planes. DRAM holds the sign, exponent and top mantissa planes. The low-order planes live in CXL-attached flash and stream in only for operations flagged as precision-critical, such as optimizer updates. It is progressive JPEG for working memory, shifting from the bit scale to the tier scale.
why: BF16/FP32 tensors need 2-3x less DRAM when most kernels run on 6-8 effective bits. It also lowers the bandwidth spent per useful bit.

title: Genotype embeddings regenerated in the memory controller
idea: Recommender embedding tables are TB-scale. Each ID is stored instead as an 8-16 byte genotype code, and a tiny shared decoder MLP in the CXL memory controller expands it into the full 128-512-dim phenotype vector in ~50 ns on read. The full table never exists in DRAM. This is a molecule-to-organism scale jump: store the recipe, not the body.
why: Embedding tables are the largest DRAM consumer in ads/recsys fleets. This gives 10-50x fewer bytes at a small accuracy cost.

title: Sub-second rack memory spot market over CXL
idea: Every 100 ms, the servers in a rack bid for 256 MB slices of pooled CXL memory. Each bid uses a price derived from that server's page-fault rate and SLO slack. An auctioneer in the switch reassigns slices, so stranded DRAM flows to whoever values it most at that instant.
why: Stranded or idle DRAM is 25-50% in clouds. Reallocating it every fraction of a second lets racks provision 20-30% less.

title: Row-buffer-sized compression blocks exploiting 8 KB overfetch
idea: DRAM activates an 8 KB row anyway, so compress at row granularity, using large-window LZ/BDI with a per-row dictionary. A row-buffer-side engine on the buffer chip or base die decompresses, while the CPU still sees 64 B lines. Compression moves up from line scale to row scale, so the overfetch becomes a free large window.
why: Large blocks compress 1.5-2x better than 64 B lines, for 1.8-2.5x effective capacity. It also puts the 128x overfetch (fact 8) to use.

title: Phylogenetic tree storage for resident model variants
idea: All fine-tuned variants resident on a node form an evolutionary tree. Each node stores 1-bit sign deltas plus per-channel scales relative to its parent, rebuilt on the fly in the GEMM epilogue. Serving 100 variants costs about one base model plus 100 x 1/16 of its size.
why: Multi-tenant serving memory falls 10-30x compared with separate copies. This extends LoRA-style sharing to full fine-tunes.

title: Fiber delay-line loop memory for strictly periodic weight streams
idea: This revives delay-line memory at datacenter scale. Weights that are read in the same order every decode step circulate in a 40 km dense-WDM fiber spool (100 wavelengths x 400 Gb/s gives about 1 GB in flight on a ~200 us loop), kept alive by optical amplifiers. Accelerators tap the stream as it passes, because sequential lockstep access never needs random addressing.
why: It replaces DRAM capacity for repeatedly streamed read-only data with roughly $5k of fiber: GB-scale capacity with no DRAM wafers.

title: Procure DRAM in touched-byte-hours, not installed gigabytes
idea: Hyperscalers and OEMs size memory contracts and server SKUs from fleet telemetry of touched GB-hours, meaning pages accessed in each 2-minute window. They buy installed DRAM at the 95th percentile of the touched set plus a compressed far tier. Part of what vendors are paid covers effective capacity delivered through compression.
why: Telemetry shows 30-50% of installed DRAM untouched for minutes at a time. Buying to the touched footprint cuts new DIMM purchases 20-35% during the shortage.

title: Cache-line-granular hot packing across cold pages
idea: A CXL controller tracks access bits per 64 B line within hot pages. It migrates the cold lines of hot pages to a compressed far tier and packs hot lines from many pages into dense hot frames through an indirection table. Tiering shifts from the 4 KB page scale to the 64 B line scale.
why: Only 20-40% of the lines in a typical hot page are hot. This needs 1.5-2x less fast DRAM for the same miss rate.

title: Sleep-consolidation pass re-encoding memory during idle troughs
idea: This borrows from how sleep consolidates memory. In nightly or between-batch idle windows, a host daemon re-encodes cold resident data with slow, strong codecs that are too expensive online: zstd-19, learned dictionaries, global dedup and struct-of-arrays relayout. Online paths only ever decompress with cheap decoders.
why: Asymmetric codecs reach 3-4x where online-speed codecs get about 2x. Spending off-peak compute shrinks daytime DRAM for cold data by 30-50%.

title: GOP-style delta frames for in-memory replicas
idea: This is video-codec thinking applied to replication. Hot-standby replicas of in-memory databases, caches or VMs keep one full I-frame replica per rack. The other replicas hold only periodic P-frame write deltas against it plus a log, and rebuild a full copy only on failover, which takes seconds.
why: In-DRAM replication factor drops from 3 to about 1.2, saving 40-60% of DRAM in replicated stores in exchange for failover time.

title: Algebraic views evaluated at the memory port
idea: Many resident tensors are cheap functions of others: GQA repeat_kv expansions, broadcasts, padding, transposes, rotary-embedded keys. Store only the base tensor plus a view descriptor, and have the load unit or a near-memory engine evaluate the view on each read. Work moves from write time to read time.
why: This removes expanded copies (up to 8x for GQA expansions) and padding, cutting activation and KV footprint by 10-40%.

title: Client-parked compressed KV state between conversation turns
idea: After each turn, the server sends the user's device or the nearest edge PoP a compressed, encrypted latent state of ~0.5-2 MB (MLA-style low-rank KV or a distilled gist-token set). The next request uploads it back. The datacenter then holds no per-session state across gaps of minutes to days.
why: The long-timescale residency of KV moves off scarce HBM/DRAM onto idle client storage. Datacenter session memory shrinks toward only the active-decode set.

title: Free in-DRAM row copy unlocks aggressive copy-on-write sharing
idea: In-subarray row copy (RowClone-style back-to-back activation) breaks copy-on-write in about 90 ns instead of a microsecond page copy over the bus. With the time cost of unsharing 10x lower, the OS shares far more aggressively: fork-heavy servers, VM clones, database snapshots, and pages with short expected sharing lifetimes.
why: When unsharing is nearly free in time, sharing pays off even for short-lived pages. That adds 10-30% to dedup savings.

title: Pod-wide HBM borrowing over the scale-up fabric
idea: In a 72-GPU NVLink-class domain, each GPU exposes its idle HBM through the fabric. KV overflow and cold weights spill to a neighbor's HBM at about 1 TB/s, so no single GPU has to be provisioned for worst-case context length. Provisioning moves from the chip scale to the pod scale.
why: Provisioning for the pod average instead of each GPU's peak needs 25-40% less HBM per accelerator at the same SLOs.

title: Predictive-coding memory storing only residuals of a tiny predictor
idea: A small fixed predictor (linear or tiny neural) in the memory controller predicts each 64 B line from its neighbors and a per-page context on every access. DRAM stores only the entropy-coded residuals. This is the brain's and video codecs' predictive coding, run at the nanosecond scale.
why: Structured data (tables, pointers, tensors) leaves small residuals, for 1.5-2.5x capacity beyond pattern-based compression.

title: Staggered garbage-collection cycles sharing one pooled heap headroom
idea: Co-located JVM, Go and .NET processes each reserve 1.5-3x their live heap as headroom. A node-level coordinator staggers their GC cycles in time and lends a single shared headroom region (memfd plus ballooning) to whichever process is about to collect.
why: Headroom is multiplexed in time instead of replicated per process, for 20-40% less DRAM on managed-language fleets.

title: Via-programmed mask ROM holding year-frozen foundation model weights
idea: A standard base die, built on a DRAM-periphery or mature logic process, adds one contact/via mask that encodes a frozen model's weights as present or absent vias. Each bit takes about 2-4 F^2 and needs no capacitor and no refresh. The dies stack HBM-style beside the accelerator, and each new model release costs just that one mask. The time-scale insight: weights stay unchanged for 6-18 months, so they need no rewritable cells.
why: Weights (30-60% of inference HBM) leave DRAM entirely. A ROM bit costs about 3x less than a DRAM bit and needs no refresh energy, all for one added mask per model version.

title: One hybrid-bond pad mask bolting a compressor onto every bank
idea: A single added Cu hybrid-bond pad mask on top of a standard DRAM wafer exposes each bank's internal data bus. A face-to-face bonded logic die compresses and decompresses per bank at internal bandwidth, so the capacity gain costs no external bandwidth. Compression moves from the CPU, centimeters away, to the bank, micrometers away.
why: About 2x effective capacity at bank-level bandwidth, with no TSVs and one mask.

title: Thick-metal coil mask enabling TSV-free stacked dedup engine
idea: One added thick top-metal mask forms inductive-coupling coils on each DRAM die. The dies stack over a logic die with no TSVs, and that logic die runs a stack-wide 64 B content-addressed dedup engine with its hash index in SRAM. Duplicate lines across all 8 dies collapse into one physical copy, so dedup moves to the stack scale.
why: It avoids the HBM TSV tax (fact 6) while adding stack-scale dedup, for 1.3-2x effective capacity on VM, container and ML workloads.

title: Offset-trim implant enabling 2-bit cells only for millisecond-lived data
idea: One added halo/Vt implant mask tightens sense-amp transistor mismatch enough for 4-level sensing. Cells store 2 bits only for data that lives shorter than the shortened MLC retention of ~4-8 ms: in-flight activations and current-step scratch. Before that deadline, the allocator demotes any surviving data to 1-bit mode. Data lifetime is matched to cell retention.
why: Ephemeral data is 20-40% of accelerator working memory. Doubling its bits per cell gives 1.2-1.4x capacity per die.

title: Single MIM-capacitor mask giving SoCs a compression-metadata eDRAM
idea: One BEOL MIM-capacitor mask added to the CPU/GPU logic process yields dense 1T1C eDRAM at about 3x SRAM density. It is used only for compressed-memory metadata and translation (sector sizes, line pointers) for all of main memory. Metadata misses, the main reason compressed DRAM is slow, disappear, so 32-64 MB of on-die storage governs a TB-scale tier.
why: It makes 2-3x main-memory compression latency-neutral, so servers can install proportionally less DRAM.

title: One-metal passive bridge letting four accelerators share HBM stacks
idea: A silicon bridge with a single metal layer (one mask, no active devices) wires each HBM stack to two to four neighboring accelerator dies through an arbiter in the HBM base die. Capacity is statistically multiplexed at the package scale instead of hard-assigned per die.
why: Peak KV demand across dies is largely uncorrelated, so package HBM can be about 25-40% smaller for the same SLO, using a near-trivial interposer.

title: Wafer stitching mask turning a DRAM wafer into shared pool
idea: One added top-metal stitching mask links reticle fields across the scribe lines, so an entire 300 mm DRAM wafer becomes one TB-scale memory fabric. Compute tiles bonded around it all read a single copy of the weights and shared KV prefixes, and defective fields are routed around.
why: Jumping from chip-scale to wafer-scale sharing collapses weight and prefix replication across 50-100 accelerators into one copy, cutting memory need 2-5x for large-model serving.

title: DRAM test-mode compare reused as in-chip dedup verifier
idea: This adds zero masks. The parallel-test compare circuitry that already sits on every DRAM die for production test is exposed as a runtime command. A candidate duplicate page is then verified bit-exact inside the DRAM in one operation, instead of streaming both copies to the CPU. A factory-time feature becomes a runtime one.
why: It removes the 2 x 4 KB of bandwidth and energy each dedup verification costs, which makes continuous fine-grained dedup cheap: 10-25% capacity savings on VM hosts.

title: Match-line metal mask makes one subarray per bank a fingerprint CAM
idea: One added metal mask lays wired-OR match lines across a dedicated subarray in each bank that stores 32-bit line fingerprints. A search broadcasts a fingerprint on the bitlines, and every matching row asserts its match line in one ~20 ns cycle. That makes 64 B dedup lookups possible inside DRAM without a CPU hash table.
why: Line-level dedup finds 1.3-2x more duplicates than page-level dedup but was impractical because of index-lookup cost. The in-DRAM CAM removes that cost.

title: Low-Vt implant mask for bank-edge LUT dequantizers
idea: One added low-Vt implant mask speeds up a strip of periphery transistors next to each bank enough to run a 16-entry LUT dequantizer at internal row speed. Weights and KV are stored at 3-4 bits and expanded to BF16 at the bank edge, so neither capacity nor external bandwidth pays for full precision.
why: 4-5x less DRAM capacity for quantized weights and KV with no host-side dequantization cost. Unmodified DRAM periphery transistors are too slow to do this.

title: Broadcast read bus killing per-bank data replication in PIM
idea: Processing-in-memory DIMMs replicate lookup tables and model parameters in every bank, because each PIM unit sees only its own bank. One added metal mask routes a die-wide broadcast read bus, so every PIM unit reads one shared copy at the moment it is fetched. Sharing moves from the bank scale to the die scale.
why: PIM replication of shared data (often 8-64x) falls to 1, freeing most PIM capacity for unique data.

title: Refresh-as-scanner computing row fingerprints for free
idea: This adds zero masks. Every row is already sensed once per 32-64 ms refresh, so a tiny CRC unit at the sense-amp edge folds each refreshed row into a signature table. That gives the OS a continuously updated map of duplicate and zero rows. The DRAM's own refresh rhythm becomes the dedup scan cycle.
why: Refresh energy (46 fJ/bit, fact 3) now does useful work, and detecting duplicate and zero rows without CPU scans reclaims 10-30% of capacity.

title: HBM base die evicts KV tokens by accumulated attention
idea: This adds zero DRAM masks; the change lives in the HBM4 custom logic base die. The base die snoops attention-score writes, keeps each token's accumulated attention in SRAM, and on its own demotes low-scoring tokens' KV to a compressed far tier while pinning attention-sink tokens. The memory itself decides what to forget, on a microsecond timescale.
why: KV footprint is 3-8x smaller at matched accuracy, and the GPU spends no cycles on eviction policy.

title: RDL side-port lets HBM time-slice between tenants in milliseconds
idea: One added redistribution-layer mask on the interposer routes a wide side-port from each HBM base die to a co-packaged flash/LPDDR tier. A tenant's entire 24 GB HBM context then swaps in about 5 ms without crossing the GPU, so HBM is time-shared among 3-4 low-duty inference tenants like CPU time slices.
why: HBM is allocated in time instead of space, so bursty low-duty serving needs 2-3x less HBM.

title: Thin-provisioned DRAM die with on-die row indirection
idea: This adds zero masks. A latch-based row indirection table in the periphery lets a die advertise about 1.5x more logical rows than it has physical rows. A physical row is allocated on the first non-zero write, and rows that are freed or zeroed through a TRIM-like command return to the pool. Virtual memory moves down to the die scale.
why: Zero or never-written memory is 10-30% of allocated footprint. Die-level thin provisioning reclaims it transparently, for 1.2-1.4x effective capacity.

title: Precision-resistor mask enabling charge-domain MAC inside commodity DDR
idea: One added thin-film resistor mask gives commodity DDR dies a calibrated charge-sharing reference, enabling bit-serial analog multiply-accumulate on the bitlines. Bandwidth-hungry decode GEMV runs inside the DDR, so weights can live in cheap DDR instead of HBM. Compute moves from the package scale to the bitline scale.
why: HBM costs about 3x the wafer area per bit (fact 6). Moving GEMV into DDR cuts HBM bits needed 2-4x and total memory wafer area per model by about 40%.

title: Fleet-trained static dictionaries burned into memory-controller firmware
idea: This adds zero masks. A dictionary of the most frequent 64 B patterns (pointers, zero runs, float templates, ELF and JIT idioms) is trained on years of fleet memory dumps and shipped yearly into controller SRAM through firmware. Every line then compresses against fleet-scale statistics instead of local history.
why: 1.3-1.6x extra compression on small lines, where local adaptive codecs fail, so hosts need less installed DRAM.

title: Depth-recurrent models reuse one block's weights across time steps
idea: This adds zero masks. Model labs train looped or depth-recurrent transformers that apply a few weight blocks repeatedly across depth, with tiny per-iteration adapters. Space (unique layers) is traded for time (iterations), paid for with compute that decode leaves idle anyway.
why: 4-8x fewer resident weight bytes at similar quality on many tasks, freeing HBM for KV.

title: Memory-efficiency label: GB-hours per transaction disclosure standard
idea: This adds zero masks. A federal cloud procurement rule, plus an Energy-Star-like label, requires software vendors and cloud services to report resident GB-hours per standard transaction or per inference token, with bid credits for each halving.
why: A years-scale incentive shift toward lean software, with 10-30% memory demand reduction across public procurement during the shortage.

title: Idle tensor cores regenerate old-context KV from token IDs
idea: This adds zero masks. Decode is memory-bound, with tensor cores ~70% idle. For context older than a horizon, the server keeps only 4-byte token IDs plus a mid-layer checkpoint every N layers, and recomputes K/V in the idle compute slots of each decode step. Nanosecond-scale compute replaces seconds-scale storage.
why: Old-context KV bytes drop 50-500x for long contexts, paid for by compute that was otherwise idle.

title: Cloud instances discounted by measured page compressibility
idea: This adds zero masks. The provider measures each tenant's compressibility and dedup ratio over a month, places compressible tenants on compressed-memory hosts, and passes back a discount. That creates a market incentive for compressible data layouts.
why: 1.5-2x effective capacity on participating hosts, lowering fleet DRAM demand 15-25%.

title: Single-mask polymer waveguide backplane for rack memory pooling
idea: One lithography mask patterns polymer optical waveguides directly into the rack backplane PCB. With existing co-packaged transceivers, they link 32 compute sleds to a shared memory sled. That makes rack-scale pooling cheap enough for each sled to ship with half its local DRAM.
why: Pooling recovers 25-50% stranded memory, so racks need 30-40% fewer DIMMs.

title: Bit-significance-partitioned refresh for approximate tensors
idea: This adds zero masks. The allocator lays out tensors so that sign, exponent and high-mantissa bits sit in different rows from low-mantissa bits. The controller refreshes high-significance rows normally and low-significance rows 8-16x less often, using per-row directed refresh. Refresh time is matched to the importance of each bit.
why: It recovers 50-80% of refresh energy and bandwidth on tensor regions (fact 3), with errors confined to LSBs: approximate memory with no new cells.
